blocks.title: Energy
blocks.text: The energy of a body is its capacity to do work. There are two basic forms of energy: (i) kinetic energy and (ii) potential energy. Kinetic energy is the energy possessed by a body due to its motion, and potential energy is the energy possessed by a body due to its changed position. Both are kinds of mechanical energy.

Let us derive a formula for the kinetic energy of a moving body. Consider a car running with constant speed on a road: if its engine is switched off it still covers some distance before stopping. As long as it moves it does work against the force of friction of the road; during this interval it exerts a force equal in magnitude to the force of friction f. If the distance travelled before coming to rest is d, the work done by the car is f d. This work is done by the car due to its motion; the ability of a body to do work due to its motion is its kinetic energy, so the kinetic energy of the car equals f d. The acceleration is found from Newton's second law, F = ma; as the car slows down and finally stops, its acceleration a is negative because it is produced by the force of friction f acting opposite to the direction of motion: f = -ma, or a = -f/m. The value of f d follows from the third equation of motion, 2aS = vf^2 - vi^2, with initial velocity vi = v, final velocity vf = 0, distance S = d and acceleration a = -f/m: 2 (-f/m) d = 0 - v^2, so f d = (1/2) m v^2. As f d equals the kinetic energy of the body, kinetic energy = (1/2) m v^2 ... (4.9). Since kinetic energy equals the work the body is capable of doing, its unit must be that of work, the joule (J).

blocks.title: Example 4.3
blocks.text: A car weighing 18620 N runs at 16 m s^-1; the brakes are applied and it is brought to rest in 80 m. Determine the average force of friction acting on it. Solution: v = 16 m s^-1, d = 80 m, w = 18620 N, f = ?. The kinetic energy of the car equals the work done by it before stopping: (1/2) m v^2 = f d. Here m = w/g = 18620 N / 9.8 m s^-2 = 1900 kg. Putting the values, (1/2) x 1900 kg x (16 m s^-1)^2 = f x 80 m, or f = 3040 N.

blocks.text: Potential energy is possessed by a body because of its position in a force field, for example the gravitational field, or because of its constrained state. The energy stored in a compressed spring is the potential energy possessed by the spring due to its compressed or stretched state; this form is called elastic potential energy.

blocks.title: Absolute gravitational potential energy
blocks.text: The absolute gravitational potential energy of an object at a certain position is the work done by the gravitational force in displacing the object from that position to infinity, where the force of gravity becomes zero.

The relation for the work done by the gravitational force or potential energy, mgh, is true only near the surface of the Earth, where the gravitational force is nearly constant. If the body is displaced through a large distance in space, say from point 1 to N (Fig. 4.11), the gravitational force does not remain constant, since it varies inversely with the square of the distance. To overcome this difficulty we divide the distance between points 1 and N into small steps each of length delta r, so that the force is practically constant within each step; the total work is then the sum of the work done during all the steps. If r1 and r2 are the distances of points 1 and 2 from the centre O of the Earth, the work done during the first step, from point 1 to point 2, is found as follows. The distance between the centre of this step and the centre of the Earth is r = (r1 + r2)/2; as r2 - r1 = delta r, r2 = r1 + delta r, hence r = (r1 + r1 + delta r)/2 = r1 + delta r / 2 ... (4.10). The gravitational force F at the centre of this step is F = G M m / r^2 ... (4.11), where m is the mass of the object, M the mass of the Earth and G the gravitational constant. Squaring Eq. 4.10, r^2 = (r1 + delta r / 2)^2 = r1^2 + 2 r1 delta r / 2 + (delta r / 2)^2; as (delta r)^2 is much smaller than r1^2 it can be neglected, hence r^2 = r1^2 + r1 delta r; putting delta r = r2 - r1, r^2 = r1^2 + r1 (r2 - r1) = r1 r2. Hence Eq. 4.11 becomes F = G M m / (r1 r2) ... (4.12).

blocks.text: As this force is assumed constant during the interval delta r, the work done is W(1 to 2) = F . delta r = F delta r cos 180 = -G M m delta r / (r1 r2); the negative sign indicates that work has to be done on the body from point 1 to 2, because the displacement is opposite to the gravitational force. Putting delta r = r2 - r1, W(1 to 2) = -G M m (r2 - r1)/(r1 r2) = -G M m (1/r1 - 1/r2). Similarly the work during the second step, from point 2 to 3, is W(2 to 3) = -G M m (1/r2 - 1/r3), and in the last step W(N-1 to N) = -G M m (1/r(N-1) - 1/rN). Hence the total work done in displacing the body from point 1 to N is W_total = W(1 to 2) + W(2 to 3) + ... + W(N-1 to N) = -G M m [(1/r1 - 1/r2) + (1/r2 - 1/r3) + ... + (1/r(N-1) - 1/rN)], which simplifies to W_total = -G M m (1/r1 - 1/rN). If point N is at an infinite distance from the Earth, rN = infinity, so 1/rN = 1/infinity = 0; hence W_total = -G M m / r1. This total work is by definition the absolute potential energy, represented by U: U = -G M m / r, the absolute value of the gravitational potential energy of a body at distance r from the centre of the Earth. When r increases U becomes less negative, that is, U increases: when we raise a body above the surface of the Earth its potential energy increases, so to raise the body to infinite distance we must do work on it equal to G M m / R, after which its potential energy becomes zero. The absolute potential energy on the surface of the Earth is found by putting r = R, the radius of the Earth: absolute potential energy = U_g = -G M m / R ... (4.13). The negative sign shows that the Earth's gravitational field for mass m is attractive; the expression gives the work or energy required to take the body out of the Earth's gravitational field, where its potential energy with respect to the Earth is zero.
